source.title: Novel dimensions of D3 receptor function: Focus on heterodimerisation, transactivation and allosteric modulation

confidence_rationale: Directly probes Q-075's named failure mode. Dopamine D2 and D3 receptors form heteromers and can transactivate -- an intervention 'selective' for D3 can recruit signalling normally coupled to D2. This WEAKENS the clean-double-dissociation prediction for the dopamine-selection (goal/salience + commitment-release) axes, while paradoxically confirming D3 has functions distinct enough to be worth separating. Logged mixed: it supports 'D3 is functionally non-redundant' but undercuts 'receptor-selective interventions produce clean, non-crossing double dissociations'.
failure_signatures: D2-D3 heteromerization + transactivation means receptor-selective ligands do not produce receptor-selective SIGNALLING; a D3-preferring drug can harness D2-coupled pathways, so a behavioural double-dissociation designed around D2-vs-D3 selectivity can be confounded at the molecular level.

If the goal/salience-coupling and commitment-release axes are both assigned to dopamine subtypes that physically cross-talk, the two axes may not remain separable under intervention -- the collapse-into-one-dimension outcome Q-075 poses as the null.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Dopamine D3 receptors form homomers and D3-D2 heteromers; within these complexes, mechanisms such as transactivation let one protomer recruit signalling normally coupled to the other, and allosteric/bitopic ligands act differently on heteromers than on monomers -- so D3 has distinctive functions but its pharmacology is entangled with D2 at the receptor-complex level.
mapping.ree_translation: Q-075 predicts the goal/salience-coupling and commitment-release axes map to dopamine-selection subtypes (D2-vs-D3, with an M4-muscarinic contribution), tested by receptor-selective double dissociation. This paper is the counterweight: it shows the molecular basis on which such a dissociation could FAIL -- D2 and D3 heteromerize and transactivate, so 'selective' interventions may not cleanly separate the two dopamine-graded axes.
mapping.mapping_caveat: OUT-OF-DOMAIN by design (V3 has no dopamine receptor subtypes; receptor rung out_of_domain per receptor_subtype_intervention_layer.md Section 4). The paper is molecular pharmacology, not a behavioural axis study; inferring axis-collapse from heteromer cross-talk is an indirect, cross-level inference. It shows a mechanism by which dissociation could fail, not that REE's specific axes do collapse.
mapping.source_context: Molecular-pharmacology review of dopamine-receptor homo/heteromerization, PET-ligand and antipsychotic/partial-agonist binding profiles, and allosteric modulation.

confidence_components.notes: Authoritative molecular review (source_quality 0.75). Cross-level inference (molecular heteromerization -> behavioural axis collapse) and out-of-domain transfer hold mapping_fidelity/transfer_risk at 0.50; value is as the honest counter-signal to the clean-dissociation prediction.
